Seminar Title:

Development of in-pack Microwave Pasteurization Process for Hot Spice Blend (Garam Masala)

Seminar Type:

Synopsis Seminar

Department:

Food Process Engineering

Speaker Name:

Chinglen Leishangthem ( Rollno : 519fp1002)

Speaker Type:

Student

Venue:

CH 113

Date and Time:

24 Jun 2026 10:30 AM

Contact:

Parag Prakash Sutar

Abstract:

Garam Masala is a mixture of ground spices commonly used in Indian and some Asian cuisines and generally has a high initial microbial load and relatively higher moisture content. Therefore, it is not shelf-stable for longer durations due to its vulnerability to microbial growth. In-pack pasteurization of Garam Masala can eliminate the risk of microbial growth in the presence of moisture and minimize the cross-contamination. In this research work, Garam Masala was heated using microwave (MW) energy under bulk and in-pack conditions. The thermal stability, quality, and microbial reduction in Garam Masala were studied by applying high-power MW (10-20 W/g) for short times (60-120 s) and low-power MW (3 W/g) for relatively longer times (4.7-6.4 min). In the high-power process, the Garam Masala in bulk condition was subjected to MW power densities of 10, 15, and 20 W/g. This process exhibited some reduction in moisture content, the total aerobic mesophilic bacterial count (2.79 log), and B. cereus(1.83 log). Total phenolic content, total flavonoid content, and antioxidant capacity were significantly enhanced in Garam Masala due to the MW heating, but the rise in the product temperature was very fast, resulting in charring through hot spots after 60 s. To avoid the problem of overheating and achieve higher microbial reduction, the Garam Masala was heated at lower power densities by placing it in a polyethylene terephthalate (PET) bottle. The Garam Masala at different initial moisture contents (10.51, 14.46, and 18.23 % wb) was packed in PET bottles, and exposed to MW at 3 W/g in continuous as well as pulsation mode until the target temperatures of 85 &degC, 95 &degC, and 105 &degC were achieved. The temperature profiles indicated that vapour generation inside the PET bottle improved the overall heating uniformity. The in-pack pasteurization resulted in a log reduction of 1.57 to 4.86 in S. enterica and 2.07 to 4.74 in B. cereus. The log-linear and Weibull models were fitted to microbial reduction data. The Weibull model was found to be the best-fitted model. The total phenolic contents and antioxidant activity in Garam Masala were also enhanced after the in-pack pasteurization. The spectral signatures of the MW-treated and untreated samples remain almost unaltered, indicating that MW treatment did not change their functional group. The optimized inpack pasteurization condition for Garam Masala was determined to be an initial moisture content of 18.23 % wb and a MW treatment at 105 ℃. Further, the sample in the PET bottle treated at optimum conditions was cooled in UV-C for 30 min to get additional microbial reduction. The optimized MW treatment combined with UV-C for 30 min achieved log reductions of 6.11 for S. enterica and 6.50 for B. cereus. The integration of UV-C treatment during the post-cooling phase has shown a synergistic effect. The combined MW and UV-C in-pack pasteurization process achieved more than 6-log reduction for both the microbes, balancing a critical safety margin with preserving quality attributes like colour, total phenolic contents, and antioxidant activity. A storage study was conducted for 3 months at 4, 25, and 35 &degC to evaluate the shelf stability of the optimized sample. The results indicated that quality was retained throughout the storage period within acceptable limits. The overall in-pack MW and UV-C in-pack pasteurization process was a scalable solution for microbial reduction and quality retention in Garam Masala.
